title: CNET AI-assisted finance explainers passed editorial review with factual errors
system_purpose: Generate explanatory finance articles for publication
decision_impact: Influenced published wording and factual explanations presented to readers as reviewed editorial content
verified_facts: Futurism inspected a CNET AI-generated compound-interest explainer and documented errors about interest earnings, loan interest and certificates of deposit. CNET corrected the article, and its correction described an additional APR-versus-APY error.
reported_harm: Actual harm verified at the publication layer was inaccurate financial information reaching readers and subsequent correction work. Futurism also reported unattributed structural and wording similarity, but that remains a reported investigation and expert opinion rather than a legal finding; no reader loss was established.
quantitative_evidence: Denominator: one inspected CNET explainer; Futurism documented three errors before contact and reported that CNET's correction identified a fourth. No valid rate for the full article set is inferred.
limitations: The model, prompts, retrieval context and editor workload were not audited. Secondary reports cannot show how many readers relied on the errors or whether similarity amounted to copyright infringement.

title: Clarkesworld temporarily closed open submissions amid suspected AI story spam
system_purpose: Use generative text tools to produce fiction submissions at high volume
decision_impact: Affected which stories entered a paying magazine's editorial review queue and whether legitimate writers could submit
verified_facts: The Guardian reported that Clarkesworld stopped considering submissions after a sharp rise in submissions its editor classified as AI-generated or plagiarized. The closure applied to all writers while the magazine sought a workable response.
reported_harm: The editorial team faced an unsustainable review burden and legitimate writers temporarily lost access to an open paying market. The editor warned that proposed barriers could disproportionately disadvantage new and international authors.
quantitative_evidence: Editor-reported counts: about 10 suspect submissions in a typical month, 100 rejected and banned in January 2023, and more than 500 by 21 February 2023; these are counts, not an independently audited AI-detection rate.
limitations: AI attribution and counts were self-reported by the editor, detectors were described as unreliable, and the source does not identify which generation products were used or measure each writer's opportunity loss.

title: Five unauthorized books were listed under Jane Friedman's name
system_purpose: Generate and sell book-like content while using an established author's identity
decision_impact: Influenced marketplace attribution, reader trust and the author's reputation before platform removal
affected_groups: Jane Friedman;readers;authors with smaller profiles;Amazon and Goodreads
verified_facts: Jane Friedman documented five titles she did not write that were credited to her; the Guardian confirmed that five falsely attributed books were listed and then removed from Amazon. The listings also appeared on Goodreads.
reported_harm: Friedman reported reputational violation, reader deception risk and the burden of policing her name. She believed the books were AI-generated based on their text and her AI-tool experience, but neither source established that provenance as a technical or legal finding.
quantitative_evidence: Five unauthorized titles were named in the first-party account and five were reported removed; no units sold, revenue, complaint rate or duration-to-removal denominator was published.
limitations: The seller and tool were not identified; AI generation was suspected, not forensically proven. The sources provide no sales or reader-harm measurements and cannot establish how a smaller-profile author would have fared.
